group.title: Culture and travel
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Friendly and generous treatment of guests and visitors.
examples: We were moved by the {hospitality} of the village families.
wrong: Their hospitality was so poor that they locked the door on every guest.

words.meaning: The accepted rules of polite behavior in a place or group.
examples: Local {etiquette} says you should remove your shoes indoors.
wrong: Shouting at the waiter is good etiquette in a fine restaurant.

words.meaning: Still natural and beautiful, not changed by building or crowds of tourists.
examples: We swam at an {unspoiled} beach with no hotels in sight.
wrong: The unspoiled coast was covered in high-rise hotels and car parks.

words.meaning: A rare or special food that people value highly.
examples: Fresh sea urchin is a local {delicacy} on the island.
wrong: Plain boiled rice is a rare delicacy that only rich people eat.

words.meaning: A stay with a local family in their home while visiting a country.
examples: My {homestay} in Spain helped me learn the language quickly.
wrong: On her homestay, she lived alone in a big hotel.

words.meaning: A long, organized journey to explore or study somewhere.
examples: The {expedition} to the North Pole took three months.
wrong: Our expedition was a short walk to the corner shop.

words.meaning: A strong wish to travel and see the world.
examples: Her {wanderlust} took her to forty countries before she was thirty.
wrong: His wanderlust made him refuse to leave his hometown ever.

words.meaning: Far from the places most tourists visit; quiet and little known.
examples: We found a lovely village {off the beaten track}.
wrong: The museum in the busy main square is completely off the beaten track.

words.meaning: A place that attracts many visitors and charges them too much.
examples: That restaurant by the cathedral is a real {tourist trap}.
wrong: The tourist trap was a cheap, quiet cafe that only locals knew.

words.meaning: A person who travels to many countries.
examples: As a {globetrotter}, he has a passport full of stamps.
wrong: The globetrotter had never been outside his own town.

words.meaning: The official office of one country’s government in another country.
examples: She went to the {embassy} to replace her lost passport.
wrong: We ordered pizza from the embassy down the street.

words.meaning: The confused feeling people get when living in a very different place.
examples: Moving from a village to Tokyo gave him real {culture shock}.
wrong: She felt culture shock when she returned to the house she grew up in.

words.meaning: Thought to be better than it really is.
examples: The famous restaurant was {overrated}; the food was ordinary.
wrong: The overrated beach was even better than everyone had said.

words.meaning: Something people in a society usually do, passed down over time.
examples: It is a {custom} here to give money in red envelopes.
wrong: The custom started yesterday and nobody follows it.

words.meaning: Something a culture forbids people to do or talk about.
examples: Talking about money at dinner is a {taboo} in some families.
wrong: Saying thank you is a strong taboo, so everyone says it.

words.meaning: Made up of people from many different cultures.
examples: London is a {multicultural} city with hundreds of languages.
wrong: The multicultural school had pupils from only one background.

words.meaning: Full of people and ideas from many parts of the world.
examples: The capital has a {cosmopolitan} feel, with food from every continent.
wrong: The cosmopolitan town had never seen a foreign visitor.

words.meaning: Pretty and charming to look at, like a painting.
examples: We stayed in a {picturesque} fishing village.
wrong: The picturesque street was ugly, dirty and full of trash.

words.meaning: Having beautiful natural views.
examples: We took the {scenic} route along the coast.
wrong: The scenic road ran through a dark tunnel with no views.

words.meaning: Unusual and exciting because it comes from a far-off place.
examples: The market sells {exotic} fruits I had never seen.
wrong: Bread and butter are exotic foods we eat every day.

words.meaning: So beautiful or impressive that it surprises you.
examples: The view from the summit was {breathtaking}.
wrong: The breathtaking view was dull and not worth a look.

words.meaning: To make a long, hard walk, often over hills or mountains.
examples: We {trekked} for five days through the Himalayas.
wrong: They trekked to the car parked by the front door.

words.meaning: A holiday spent at home or near where you live.
examples: Instead of flying abroad, we had a {staycation} and explored our own city.
wrong: Our staycation was a month-long trip to the other side of the world.

words.meaning: A place or thing so good that everyone should visit it.
examples: The old castle is a {must-see} for anyone visiting the city.
wrong: The museum is a must-see, so nobody should bother going.

words.meaning: Sudden rough movement of air that shakes a plane.
examples: Please fasten your seatbelts; we are expecting some {turbulence}.
wrong: The flight was perfectly smooth because of the turbulence.

words.meaning: On the way to a place.
examples: We stopped for lunch {en route} to the airport.
wrong: We had dinner en route, long after we had arrived home.

words.meaning: To get used to a new climate or place.
examples: It took us three days to {acclimatize} to the heat.
wrong: He acclimatized so badly that he felt at home in the heat at once.

words.meaning: To tell customs officers about goods you are bringing into a country.
examples: You must {declare} any cash over ten thousand dollars.
wrong: He declared the watch by hiding it in his sock.

words.meaning: To get onto a ship or plane at the start of a journey.
examples: Passengers will {embark} at the main harbor at noon.
wrong: We embarked the ship as soon as it reached its final port.

words.meaning: To get off a ship or plane at the end of a journey.
examples: We {disembarked} and walked into the arrivals hall.
wrong: The passengers disembarked before the ship left the first harbor.

words.meaning: To travel around without a fixed plan or route.
examples: We spent a week {roaming} the hills of Tuscany.
wrong: He roamed the city by staying in his hotel room all week.

words.meaning: Very far away, in a distant part of the world.
examples: She sends postcards from {far-flung} islands in the Pacific.
wrong: We visited a far-flung village just across the road.

words.meaning: Travel to natural places that tries to protect the environment and help local people.
examples: {Ecotourism} brings money to the rainforest without cutting down trees.
wrong: The ecotourism company paved over the wetland to build a car park.

words.meaning: A journey to a holy or special place for religious or personal reasons.
examples: Every year, thousands make the {pilgrimage} to the ancient temple.
wrong: His pilgrimage was a quick trip to buy groceries.

words.meaning: A holy place built to honor a god, saint or important person.
examples: Visitors leave flowers at the small roadside {shrine}.
wrong: The shrine is a busy shop where people buy cheap toys.

words.meaning: Full of busy, noisy activity.
examples: We explored the {bustling} night market.
wrong: The bustling street was silent and completely empty.

words.meaning: Attractive in an unusual or old-fashioned way.
examples: The town is full of {quaint} little cottages.
wrong: The quaint village was full of new glass office towers.

words.meaning: Real and true to the original style, not made for tourists.
examples: This cafe serves {authentic} local dishes.
wrong: The authentic market sold only cheap fake copies.

words.meaning: A place that is very popular with visitors at the moment.
examples: The old harbor has become a tourist {hotspot}.
wrong: The hotspot was a town that no tourist ever visited.

words.meaning: Extra money given to someone for good service.
examples: A ten percent {gratuity} is added to the bill.
wrong: The gratuity was a fine the waiter had to pay us.
